metadata.title: The Survey of Adult Skills: Reader’s Companion, Third Edition

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This volume is a design/methodology companion for the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) and does not report an analytic student-level predictive model with an explicit estimation sample. It describes how PIAAC measures adult literacy, numeracy, and problem solving in technology-rich environments, and how these relate to other OECD assessments such as PISA. The document includes methodological discussion of proficiency scaling (e.g., response probability thresholds for locating individuals/items on literacy/numeracy scales) rather than a results section with a weighted regression/ML pipeline. For analysts using PIAAC microdata, complex survey design and sampling weights are typically part of the official data products; however, this specific text does not specify weight variable names or replicate-weight procedures for a particular empirical analysis.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a reader’s companion describing assessment design, construct definitions, and relationships between PIAAC and other surveys (e.g., PISA), not an empirical study that estimates a PV-based cognitive outcome for a predictive target. Because there is no reported dependent variable derived from PIAAC plausible values and no model-based missing-data strategy, PV handling and missing-data handling are not applicable/available in the sense required for an empirical ML extraction. Any missing-data or PV procedures would be implemented in the underlying PIAAC scoring/technical documentation rather than in this narrative companion chapter.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD reader’s companion (third edition) explains how the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) conceptualises and measures key information-processing skills—literacy/reading, numeracy/mathematical literacy, and problem solving in technology-rich environments—and how these relate to other OECD assessments, especially PISA. It provides framework-level comparisons (e.g., differences in target populations: adults vs. 15-year-old students) and discusses why direct score comparisons across PIAAC and PISA require caution due to different scale definitions and reporting conventions. The annexes further document how proficiency levels and descriptors are defined using response probability thresholds (e.g., RP67 vs RP80) and how literacy/numeracy scales differ from earlier adult literacy surveys (IALS/ALL). No student-level predictive modelling, performance metrics, or PV/missing-data handling for an empirical analysis are reported in the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The provided content is a methodological/relationship companion rather than an empirical ML paper: it does not define an analytic dataset with a model, target variable, or reported predictive performance. Consequently, fields such as total sample size, country-level Ns, PV handling for a specific outcome, missing-data handling for an estimation procedure, and ML algorithms are not populated because the text focuses on assessment design, construct definitions, and cross-survey comparability rather than on estimating effects or predictive accuracy.
